You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The first bench Daniel installed faced a brick wall.

He checked the work order twice. There was the address, the diagram, the small black arrow indicating the direction of the seat. Behind him stood a perfectly respectable park: plane trees, a pond, a statue of a man whose achievements had outlasted everybody’s interest in them. In front of him stood a wall.

He called his supervisor.

“Is there a reason?”

“There’s always a reason,” she said. “It’s not always on the form.”

So he drilled the holes.

By eleven, the bench was secured. He swept the dust into a neat gray pile and stood back. It looked like a punishment somebody had forgotten to administer.

An old man approached carrying two paper cups.

“You’ve finished.”

“Apparently.”

The man handed him a coffee.

“Was this your request?” Daniel asked.

“Yes.”

“You know it faces the wall.”

“I was quite specific about that.”

Daniel drank. The coffee was sweet enough to hurt his teeth.

The old man sat at the left end of the bench, leaving room beside him. He wore a brown suit with shining elbows and shoes that had been repaired more carefully than they had originally been made.

“What used to be here?” Daniel asked.

“A cinema.”

“Before my time.”

“Before most things.”

Across the street, a delivery driver argued with a parking meter. Somewhere in the park, a child was explaining the rules of a game to another child who had already decided not to follow them.

“My wife worked in the ticket booth,” the man said. “I used to wait outside until her shift finished.”

Daniel looked at the wall. There were pale rectangles where signs had once hung.

“Did you go to the films?”

“Not often. We were saving.”

“For what?”

The man considered this.

“At first, a washing machine.”

“And after that?”

“A better washing machine.”

Daniel laughed. The man smiled into his cup.

“People imagine their parents had grand ambitions. Sometimes we just wanted the sheets to come out less wet.”

That afternoon, Daniel installed three ordinary benches facing ordinary things.

He found himself annoyed by them.

***

The old man came every Thursday.

Daniel knew because Thursday was inspection day. He drove through the district with a clipboard, checking for loose bolts, splintered wood, graffiti. The work required him to sit briefly on every bench. His supervisor called this load testing. His brother called it the best job in the country.

At the wall, the old man always had two coffees.

His name was Arthur. His wife had been named June.

“She hated June,” he said one week.

“Her own name?”

“The month. Too many weddings. She said nobody should make promises while the weather was flattering them.”

Another Thursday, Arthur brought a photograph. June stood inside the ticket booth, one hand raised against the camera.

“She looks annoyed.”

“She was. I’d told her to smile.”

“Did she?”

“Not that afternoon.”

Daniel looked closely. Behind her was a board advertising a film he recognized from television.

“My mother loved that one.”

“Everyone loved that one. June said the ending was dishonest.”

“Was it?”

Arthur took the photograph back.

“I don’t remember the ending.”

***

In November, Arthur stopped coming.

Daniel arrived with his clipboard and found the bench wet, empty, and scattered with leaves. He checked the bolts. He sat down.

The following week, he brought two coffees, then felt foolish and drank both.

He thought about asking the council for Arthur’s address. He thought about whether that would be permitted. He thought about it long enough that it became the thing he had done instead of asking.

December arrived with early darkness.

Someone sprayed a silver crown on the wall. Someone else drew a door beneath it.

Daniel reported the graffiti. It was washed off within forty-eight hours.

He regretted reporting the door.

***

In January, a woman was sitting on the bench.

She had Arthur’s eyes and June’s expression from the photograph.

“You must be the bench man,” she said.

Daniel nodded.

“I’m his daughter.”

“I’m sorry.”

She rubbed a gloved hand along the armrest.

“He didn’t die.”

“Oh.”

“He fell. Then there was a hospital stay, and an argument about stairs. He’s living with me now.”

“That’s good.”

“It is, depending on which of us you ask.”

She handed Daniel an envelope.

Inside was a photograph of Arthur sitting in a kitchen, looking offended by a slice of cake. On the back, in uneven handwriting, he had written:

*The coffee here is terrible. Otherwise acceptable.*

Daniel laughed.

“He asked me to give you that,” she said. “And to tell you something about the cinema.”

“What?”

“She wasn’t my mother. June.”

He looked again at the wall.

“They were engaged before the war. It didn’t work out. He met my mother later.”

Daniel put the photograph back in its envelope.

“So why—”

“I asked him.” She pulled her scarf higher. “He said he waited here a lot.”

***

The bench remained.

On inspection days, Daniel tightened what needed tightening and picked litter from beneath the seat. Once, he found a bus ticket tucked between two slats. Once, a blue mitten no larger than a plum.

In March, somebody drew another door on the wall.

This one had a round handle, three hinges, and a little crooked mail slot. Daniel stood in front of it with the graffiti report open on his phone.

Then he closed the report.

He sat on the bench to complete the inspection. A woman walking past slowed, looked at the wall, and looked at him.

“What’s there?” she asked.

“Used to be a cinema.”

“Is that why the bench faces that way?”

Daniel shifted to check the last bolt.

“Somebody asked for it,” he said.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A restrained literary story uses a bench facing a wall to connect an ordinary worker with an old man’s memories and unfinished grief.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and dryly tender, finding pathos in practical details: coffee sweet enough to hurt, repaired shoes, a wet empty bench. Daniel’s connection with Arthur grows through repeated visits and small gestures rather than explicit declarations. The story invites the reader to treat ordinary objects as places where private histories gather, while leaving some of that history unresolved.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds benches, walls, photographs, coffee, and drawn doors as modest objects that hold memory and invite interpretation. Its moral emphasis is gentle: attentive care can mean choosing not to erase something, or simply making room for another person’s story. The recurring door and the final exchange give the ending a quiet sense of possibility without turning the loss into a tidy lesson.

## Evidence line
> It looked like a punishment somebody had forgotten to administer.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring bench-and-wall motif and the story’s controlled, understated tenderness make this a distinctive, coherent expressive choice.
